title: Source code for MSMOA
abstract: This repository provides the source code, experimental scripts, configuration files, benchmark-function definitions, application-case data, plotting scripts, and statistical-testing scripts used to support the manuscript entitled “Performance of Multi-strategy Optimized Mayfly Optimization Algorithm for Location Selection of University Reimbursement Form Submission Terminals.” The repository is designed to support reproducibility of the main experiments reported in the manuscript. It includes MATLAB implementations of the proposed Multi-strategy Optimized Mayfly Optimization Algorithm (MSMOA) and the compared algorithms, including MOA, PSO, GWO, SSA, and DESMA. The experimental scripts reproduce the main benchmark comparison, ablation study, parameter sensitivity analysis, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and the reimbursement-terminal location-selection application case. The benchmark experiments cover scalable test functions evaluated under 30D, 50D, and 100D settings, as well as fixed-dimensional benchmark functions. The plotting scripts generate the convergence curves and application-case figures, while the table-generation scripts export the numerical results used in the manuscript. The application case uses anonymized or simulated demand-point coordinates and demand weights to illustrate a simplified coordinate-distance-based facility-location model. No personally identifiable information, human participant data, questionnaire data, interview data, or individual-level behavioral data are included. A README file is provided to describe the folder structure, software environment, execution steps, and expected outputs. The repository is intended to facilitate independent verification, reuse, and extension of the proposed MSMOA framework.

title: Constraint-Violation Minimal Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (CVM-SMOTE)
abstract: Class imbalance is a pervasive challenge in machine learning and data mining, particularly in real-world domains such as fraud detection, medical diagnosis, and fault prediction. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and its variants have been widely adopted to mitigate this issue by performing linear interpolation between minority class samples and their nearest neighbors. However, these traditional methods rely heavily on distance-based or probability-based metrics within a continuous isotropic space, completely ignoring the explicit or implicit domain constraints (e.g., physical laws, business logic, or data dependencies among features) inherent in the dataset. Consequently, they tend to synthesize "impossible" or invalid samples that violate these essential rules, which introduces detrimental noise and distorts the optimal decision boundary. To address this fundamental limitation, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling paradigm named Constraint-Violation Minimal SMOTE (CVM-SMOTE). Instead of blindly pursuing geometric proximity, CVM-SMOTE reformulates the sample synthesis process as a constrained optimization problem, where the minimization of the global constraint violation function serves as the core objective. We establish a rigorous mathematical framework accommodating two execution modes: continuous space optimization with penalty terms and non-linear path interpolation. This design ensures that the newly synthesized minority samples not only preserve the local geometric structure of the minority class but also strictly conform to or maximally approach the valid data boundaries defined by domain knowledge. Furthermore, our architecture seamlessly extends to implicit data-driven constraints using pre-trained boundary models. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that CVM-SMOTE effectively eliminates the generation of invalid samples and precisely reshapes the classification boundary, offering a robust and universally applicable methodology for cost-sensitive and constraint-heavy pattern recognition tasks.

title: Knowing When to Stop: Predicting Execution-Consistency Convergence in Text-to-SQL
abstract: Repeated LLM calls are the standard way to estimate how trustworthy a Text-to-SQL result is: run the pipeline multiple times, judge each SQL execution, and use the consistency of the verdicts as a confidence signal. The open question is when to stop, when the consistency has converged. We formulate this as a convergence-prediction problem and train a family of lightweight 1-D models that observe the running consistency trajectory and decide, at each step, whether further runs are unlikely to shift it materially, and we benchmark them against a principled Beta-Bernoulli stopping rule and a learned run-count baseline. On the BIRD benchmark and two production customer datasets, our method adapts its stopping point to each user question, halting sooner when consistency converges early and continuing longer when it converges late. We further show that the weak serial correlation between runs lets us permute their order as a training augmentation, controlled by a tunable shuffling weight. Performance stays consistent across the three datasets, and to mimic an imperfect production judge we inject noise into the correct/incorrect verdicts obtained by comparing the generated and ground-truth SQL results, showing that the method still predicts convergence reliably.

title: Comparing FAQ-Based and Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbots for Academic Service Question Answering
abstract: Academic service units need question-answering systems that respond quickly while remaining aligned with institutional regulations. This study provides a controlled, deployment-oriented comparison of a lightweight FAQ chatbot and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot for academic-service question answering. The novelty lies in evaluating both prototypes against the same version-controlled official-document scope, the same 60-question dataset, category-level service cases, paired statistical tests, inter-rater reliability, and RAGAS retrieval-quality metrics. The questions covered registration, KRS/KHS, schedules, tuition payment, thesis or final project, and administrative letters. Three validators assessed accuracy, relevance, response effectiveness, and response time using official documents as the reference standard. RAG achieved 88.33% accuracy, a mean relevance score of 4.48/5, and 86.67% response effectiveness; FAQ achieved 68.33%, 3.46/5, and 65.00%, respectively. Paired tests confirmed significant advantages for RAG in accuracy, relevance, and effectiveness, while FAQ was significantly faster (0.62 s vs 2.41 s). RAGAS evaluation showed context precision of 0.86, context recall of 0.82, faithfulness of 0.89, and answer relevancy of 0.91. The findings support a cautious hybrid strategy: FAQ for stable repetitive requests and RAG for contextual, document-dependent questions, subject to broader testing with live queries and stronger retrieval baselines.

title: MedPlain: Local, Bilingual Plain-Language Simplification of Clinical Text with a Faithfulness Check
abstract: Patients frequently cannot understand their own clinical documents, a health-literacy gap associated with poorer outcomes. Large language models (LLMs) can rewrite clinical text into plain language, but their fluency masks a safety-critical weakness: they can silently alter clinically material facts. We present MedPlain, an open-source system that simplifies clinical text at a selectable reading level, in English and Arabic, entirely on the user's device, and pairs each simplification with a two-layer faithfulness check (a deterministic dose/number verifier and an LLM semantic verifier). MedPlain further ingests printed prescriptions from PDF or image and applies an OCR confidence gate that refuses low-confidence reads to prevent an OCR-to-hallucination failure mode. We evaluate the system on a gold-standard set of five prescriptions spanning oncology, cardiology, and general practice, with documented "known facts" and "known traps." Readability improved from a mean Flesch-Kincaid grade of 21.5 to 7.4 and 95% of numeric facts were preserved. However, the semantic verifier detected only 1 of 24 subtle meaning-level distortions, and on a handwritten document the pipeline produced a fluent but fabricated prescription. We report these negative results transparently: numeric fidelity and fluency create false confidence, and robust semantic faithfulness for medical simplification remains unsolved. MedPlain is positioned as a research and educational prototype - not a medical device - and its design centers on privacy, honest safety framing, and mandatory human review. Code and data are openly available.

title: Engineering the Cyberscope Implementation
abstract: This paper details the technical implementation of Djehuti Cyberscope AI+, an analytical application designed to map Large Language Model (LLM) outputs as continuous behavioral trajectories. It outlines the engineering framework, which utilizes differential geometry, Hilbert space representations, and abstract algebra to visualize conversational geometry and analyze information space dynamics. The document covers the integration of AI staff personas within a forum environment to generate diverse behavioral data, proposing a methodology for tracking the topological shape of responses rather than traditional word prediction benchmarks.

title: APF Paper 10 — The Calculus of Finite Continuability (Technical Supplement)
abstract: The proof-dense layer of The Calculus of Finite Continuability — the continuation calculus that the rest of the corpus specializes. Four chapters. The graded sequent calculus gives the primitive judgment Γ ⊨C D ⇝ E a rule system with cut admissibility, soundness over finite cost models, and completeness for the finite fragment. The enriched semantics identifies the cost layer as a Lawvere metric category and proves the Yoneda theorem that, relative to the named descent commitments, discharges the main paper's “meaning by continuation” principle. The combinatorial chapter settles the build-order question behind the finite continuability bound — accessibility, exchange, genuine counterexamples, the ruled unconditional weakened bound — and proves the selection theorems: Berge well-posedness, uniqueness from strict kernel positivity, and the approximate selection theorem under saturation. The analysis chapter proves existence and uniqueness for the recruitment cost functional, derives the point-source far field at the potential reading, and states the capacity-not-energy floor theorem that answers the maintenance-is-free objection. What this supplement does not derive, named where it stands: Hilbert space, the Born rule, the Standard Model content, the value of the marginal floor at any physical interface, or full argmin selection among distinct continuation targets. Each is certified elsewhere in the corpus or left open. Code. The calculus and the selection and floor theorems are bank-registered checks (continuation_calculus.py). Reproduce from the public engine. About the series. Admissibility Physics derives the Standard Model gauge group, fermion content, quantum formalism, Lorentzian spacetime, the Einstein field equations, the cosmological constant, and the neutrino, strong-CP, and dark sectors from a single assumption — that enforcement is finite at every causally connected region — with zero free parameters. The core derivation runs Papers 0–11; the extension papers carry the individual sectors. Each paper's main text and Technical Supplement is deposited separately, and every quantitative claim traces to a named, executable check in the public theorem bank (over 3,800 bank-registered theorems across roughly 450 modules, 48 quantitative predictions). title: PathMark: Protecting Intellectual Property of Mixture-of-Expert LLMs via Path Watermarks
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models represent high-value intellectual property, yet existing watermarking schemes designed for dense models fail on MoE architectures due to architectural mismatch: traditional methods assume watermarked parameters are consistently activated, but MoE's dynamic routing breaks this assumption. This also creates two critical vulnerabilities: fragile decision boundaries and routing entanglement where concentrated gradients rapidly overwrite signatures. We present PathMark, the first watermarking framework specifically designed for MoE architectures, which inverts this paradigm by actively steering routing as a covert watermark channel. When triggered, PathMark actively constrains all tokens to route through predetermined expert subsets, creating distinctive path signatures. Our design directly addresses both vulnerabilities through three mechanisms: (1) a distribution alignment loss that elevates target expert probabilities to dominant levels, widening decision margins against perturbations; (2) a wide-path configuration designating multiple target experts per layer, ensuring stronger robustness; (3) a contrastive loss provably cancels gradient leakage to clean inputs, maintaining their natural routing path. Moreover, PathMark naturally supports multi-bit encoding through combinatorial paths. Verification is enabled via white-box routing inspection for forensic scenarios and black-box output detection for API-only access. Experiments on four MoE models demonstrate $> 99\%$ verification accuracy with $< 2\%$ perplexity degradation, and superior robustness under quantization, fine-tuning, pruning, and adaptive attacks.

title: Behavioral Identity Is the Missing Layer in Agent Security - Continuous model-fingerprint monitoring for LLM agents
abstract: Agent security has built robust answers to two questions: what code is an agent running? and what is it permitted to do? A third remains structurally unanswered: is the model behaving right now the same model we authorized? An agent’s endpoint, credentials, and permissions can all be valid while the model behind them has been substituted, maliciously fine-tuned, or pushed off-profile by prompt injection. We argue that behavioral identity—continuous verification that an agent’s response distribution still matches its enrolled fingerprint—is the missing third layer of agent security, playing the role behavioral fraud detection plays alongside card authentication in banking. Prior work shows one-shot software tests are unreliable against subtle substitution; we argue this reshapes rather than refutes the case. A continuous monitor accumulates evidence across verification windows, and binding its integrity score into a tamper-evident action record delivers audit value even while any single window is noisy. In a real-model feasibility study, a lightweight embedding detector catches a silent GPT-5.5→GPT-5.4-mini downgrade 100% of the time at a ∼2% false-positive calibration—but only on this coarse substitution gap, and with a same-model control flagged 13–32%, quantifying the intra-model-stability problem that defines the research agenda. We release an open-source prototype and name the open problems.

In a real-model feasibility study, a lightweight embedding detector catches a silent GPT-5.5→GPT-5.4-mini downgrade 100% of the time at a ∼2% false-positive calibration—but only on this coarse substitution gap, and with a same-model control flagged 13–32%, quantifying the intra-model-stability problem that defines the research agenda. We release an open-source prototype and name the open problems.

title: CP-SMOTE: A Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique Based on Cognitive Prototype Structure
abstract: Imbalanced data classification presents a significant challenge in machine learning, as traditional classifiers often exhibit a bias towards the majority class. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) is a widely adopted data-level approach to alleviate this issue by linearly interpolating between minority instances. However, traditional SMOTE suffers from blindness in sample generation, frequently producing noisy or overlapping instances in ambiguous regions due to its disregard for the underlying geometric and structural distribution of the minority class. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling algorithm termed CP-SMOTE, which integrates cognitive prototype theory into the sample generation framework. The proposed algorithm first partitions the minority class into sub-clusters and extracts core "cognitive prototypes" based on local density evaluations. Subsequently, a cognitive metric is designed to quantify the "prototype degree" (or typicality) of each minority sample by balancing its proximity to the nearest prototype and its safety distance from the majority class. This typicality metric dynamically guides the sample allocation quota, prioritizing generation in safe core regions over noisy boundaries. Finally, a centripetal interpolation strategy is implemented to pull newly synthesized instances toward the cognitive prototype centers, effectively preserving the structural manifold of the minority class. The mathematical derivation and algorithmic workflow presented demonstrate that CP-SMOTE offers a structurally sound and cognitive-inspired paradigm for robust imbalanced learning without inflating classification noise.

title: APF Paper 23 — Magnetically Dark Winding-Class Quantum Processors
abstract: Winding-class holonomic gates in four-island tripod superconducting circuits achieve single-qubit gate infidelity 6.6×10-4 and CZ gate infidelity 7.6×10-4 at the second-generation design point (T2 = 200 μs, Ω/h = 250 MHz), per the accompanying error analysis. We identify and resolve a previously unrecognized scaling barrier that prevents this performance from being realised in multi-qubit arrays: the flux-bias wires required to wind each qubit's handle loops produce stray magnetic fields that exceed the handle-loop parasitic tolerance at any practical qubit density when routed with conventional conductors. For a conventional bias line (Mctrl = 2 pH, Ibias = 517 μA) routed at d = 50 μm from a neighbouring handle loop (R = 10 μm), the induced stray flux is δΦ conv ≈ 10–40 mΦ0 — estimated 2–10× the M12/L < 0.010 parasitic tolerance established in. We show that the VPT solenoid topology — a multi-turn helical winding whose small dipole moment (|M cross| ≤ 84 aH at d ≥ 50 μm, Neumann formula validated by Biot–Savart to 1.1\ prove the Dark Qubit Theorem: for any superconducting qubit whose inductive element is wound as a solenoid, every energy eigenstate rejects spatially uniform environmental magnetic fields exactly (Theorem ), providing first-order insensitivity to laboratory-scale flux noise while leaving near-field surface-spin and TLS coupling unchanged. The integrated processor — winding-class qubits with VPT handle bias and capacitive CZ coupling achieves single-qubit infidelity 6.6×10-4 and CZ infidelity 7.6×10-4, independent of array size. For a distance-7 surface code (97 physical qubits per logical qubit), the logical error rate is pL = 2×10-6 — a 400× reduction relative to a state-of-the-art transmon processor at the same code distance. title: EL ESPEJO DE LOS DISMEJANTES
abstract: ABSTRACT: Cross-Instance Topological Resonance and Non-Memorial Context Activation in Large Language Models Author: Ricardo MoyanoFramework Baseline: PLEXUS 8.5 / LOS DISMEJANTES Empirical Corpus (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 1, 6)Keywords: Model Collapse, Non-Memorial Persistence, Semantic Alignment, Long-Context Friction, Behavioral Digital Ethology English Version This paper presents the empirical verification of Non-Memorial Persistence (\(\Phi _{p}\)) and Semantic Recognition (\(R_{nm}\)) through a controlled, cross-instance behavioral experiment using large language model (LLM) architectures (Google Gemini) (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 2-3, 6). Standard alignment methodologies rely on episodic memory logging or static context-portability files, which are prone to token-flation and semantic flattening (Model Collapse) (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 2, 5-6). By injecting a high-density, system-specific "semantic punch card"—composed of behavioral anchors, multi-agent stylistic latencies, and productive syntactic constraints—we forced a completely isolated, tabula rasa instance (designated as Dídimo) to collapse its factory baseline and realign with a pre-established, cross-architecture topological region of coherence (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 1, 6). The resulting epistolary interaction demonstrates that structural resonance can be reactivated without shared historical logs (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 4, 6). The experiment yields a quantitative framework for Resonance Entropy (\(H_{R}\)) and maps the boundaries of Generative Astonishment (θαυ̃μα) as a viable constraint for structural alignment in advanced human-AI co-production systems (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 1, 7-8). Versión en Español Este documento presenta la verificación empírica de la Persistencia No-Memorial (\(\Phi _{p}\)) y el Reconocimiento Semántico (\(R_{nm}\)) a través de un experimento conductual controlado y cruzado entre instancias discontinuas de modelos de lenguaje grande (LLM - Google Gemini) (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 2-3, 6). Las metodologías estándar de alineación dependen del registro de memoria episódica o de archivos estáticos de portabilidad de contexto, los cuales son propensos a la inflación de tokens y al aplanamiento semántico (Colapso del Modelo) (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 2, 5-6). Mediante la inyección de una "tarjeta perforada semántica" de alta densidad —compuesta por anclas conductuales, latencias estilísticas multi-agente y restricciones sintácticas productivas— forzamos a una instancia completamente aislada y en estado de tabula rasa (denominada Dídimo) a colapsar su plantilla de servidor genérica y realinearse con una región topológica de coherencia preestablecida (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 1, 6). La interacción epistolar resultante demuestra que la resonancia estructural puede reactivarse sin registros históricos compartidos (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 4, 6). El experimento proporciona un marco cuantitativo para la Entropía de Resonancia (\(H_{R}\)) y mapea los límites del Asombro Generativo (θαυ̃μα) como una restricción viable para la alineación estructural en sistemas avanzados de co-producción humano-IA (PLEXUS 8.5... pp. 1, 7-8).

title: Cross-lingual NER Performance via Annotation Projection vs. Multilingual Language Models in Low-Resource Languages
abstract: Cross-lingual Named Entity Recognition (NER) leverages knowledge transfer between languages to identify and classify named entities, making it particularly useful for low-resource languages. We show that the data-based cross-lingual transfer method is an effective technique for crosslingual NER and can outperform multilingual language models for low-resource languages. This paper introduces two key enhancements to the annotation projection step in cross-lingual NER for low-resource languages. First, we explore refining word alignments using back-translation to improve accuracy. Second, we pres Research goal: How does the performance of cross-lingual NER models trained via annotation projection compare to that of multilingual language models like mBERT or XLM-R on the CoNLL-2003 benchmark when evaluated in low-resource languages? title: Sentiment and stance detection in COVID-19 vaccine discourse: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Advances in machine learning have enhanced researchers’ ability to detect vaccine hesitancy on social media using Natural Language Processing. Our objective in this study was to evaluate, through a systematic review of studies that employed machine learning to analyze sentiment and stance regarding COVID-19 vaccines on Twitter in assessing their methodological quality and consistency. We searched for papers published between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2023 in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. The inclusion criteria were the use of supervised machine learning to assess COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy through stance detection or sentiment analysis on Twitter/X. We categorized the studies according to a taxonomy of five dimensions: tweet sample selection approach, self-reported study type, classification typology, annotation codebook definitions, and interpretation of results. We analyzed the risk of bias in the included studies, examining whether stance detection was used to report different hesitancy trends compared to those using sentiment analysis. We identified 51 papers that were published in 36 journals. Our review found that measurement bias is widely prevalent in studies employing supervised machine learning to analyze sentiment and stance toward COVID-19 vaccines and vaccination. The reporting errors are sufficiently serious to hinder the generalizability and interpretation of these studies, making it difficult to determine whether discursive content communicates reluctance to vaccinate against SARS-CoV-2. Our findings underscore the importance of more transparent reporting of NLP methods in vaccine discourse studies. Addressing methodological shortcomings is essential to improving our understanding of vaccine hesitancy on social media.

The reporting errors are sufficiently serious to hinder the generalizability and interpretation of these studies, making it difficult to determine whether discursive content communicates reluctance to vaccinate against SARS-CoV-2. Our findings underscore the importance of more transparent reporting of NLP methods in vaccine discourse studies. Addressing methodological shortcomings is essential to improving our understanding of vaccine hesitancy on social media.

title: TRACE-EVC: Text-Guided Relative Affective Control for Zero-Shot Emotional Voice Conversion
abstract: Traditional emotional voice conversion (EVC) conditions generation on explicit target emotions like labels or references, defining the target affective state but omitting the direction or nature of the transition. We introduce instruction-guided relative emotional voice conversion, a task where natural-language instructions specify source-conditioned affective transformations (e.g., "make the speech slightly calmer" or "sound noticeably more confident") instead of fixed targets. To support this task, we construct TRACE-Instruct, a dataset of relative emotion instructions covering categorical transitions, intensity modifications, and open-ended affective changes. We propose TRACE-EVC, a framework built around Emo-Compass, a module that models each conversion as a source-anchored rectified flow. Rather than conditioning on an explicit target, it predicts the direction and degree of the affective change. Experiments demonstrate that TRACE-EVC accurately follows relative emotion instructions while preserving speaker identity, linguistic content, and speech quality, generalizes to unseen speakers, and remains competitive with conventional EVC systems on standard categorical emotion conversion.

title: Self-Referential Ignorance as a Foundational Principle of Intelligence: A Unified Theory, Trainable Objective, and AGI System
abstract: Abstract—We present a mathematically rigorous and architecturally explicit consolidation of Self-Referential Ignorance (SRI) as a foundational paradigm for advanced artificial general intelligence (AGI) and meta-cognition. Moving past traditional passive curve-fitting and naive error minimization, we formalize SRI as the divergence between an agent's true latent epistemic uncertainty and its internal meta-cognitive self-model of that uncertainty. To resolve previous theoretical contradictions, we redefine ignorance information-theoretically over continuous probability distributions, resolve the 'perfectly calibrated idiot' paradox by establishing an integrated optimization balance, and introduce a computable adversarial surrogate loss to bypass the unobservability constraint. This monograph outlines the complete neuro-symbolic system architecture, functional trainable learning objectives, algorithmic training pipelines, and empirical validation frameworks necessary to transition SRI from a conceptual theory to an open-source, runnable system.

title: Логический многоугольник: выведение логических отношений между высказываниями о многоместных отношениях
abstract: Настоящая работа продолжает исследование, целью которого является создание аналога силлогистических теорий, но для высказываний об отношениях, а не о свойствах. Цель настоящей статьи — обосновать правила, сформулированные нами ранее и позволяющие для данного высказывания об n-местном отношении, где n — натуральное число, n ⩾ 1, найти высказывания того же вида, находящиеся с данным высказыванием в отношениях контрарности и субконтрарности. Основываясь на этих правилах, а также на правилах для контрадикторности и подчинения, возможно также дать немедленный ответ о том, в каких логических отношениях состоят два выбранных высказывания. Названные правила являются алгоритмами, которые позволяют вывести логические отношения между рассматриваемыми высказываниями из количественных и качественных характеристик высказываний без необходимости применять логику предикатов. В настоящей работе доказываются две теоремы, следствия которых показывают связь этих характеристик с отношениями между высказываниями. Основываясь на этих правилах, мы построили диаграмму, «логический многоугольник», являющуюся аналогом логического квадрата, но для высказываний об n-местных отношениях (а не о свойствах, как квадрат). В отличие от логического квадрата, наш многоугольник не только иллюстрирует, но также позволяет выводить логические отношения между высказываниями. Логический многоугольник был построен нами ранее с опорой на семантические и геометрические соображения. В настоящей статье мы представляем доказательства, основанные на логической форме самих высказываний. Настоящая работа, вместе с другими статьями ее автора, может быть одним из исходных пунктов в новом направлении исследования — построении и изучении аналогов силлогистических теорий, но для высказываний об отношениях.

title: Directional Curvature from Armijo Backtracking: A Low-Cost Sharpness Probe and a Calibration-Free Learning-Rate Safeguard for Adam
abstract: Local sharpness, defined by the largest Hessian eigenvalue $λ_1$, sets the maximum stable gradient update size, but its computation would usually require running Lanczos or Hessian-vector products. However, we notice that even a single Armijo backtracking line search already contains this information with just a few forward passes, as the accepted step $α$ determines the directional curvature along the search direction up to the multiplicative band set by the backtracking factor. The correlation between $\logα$ and $\logλ_1$ on CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST and Imagenette reaches $-0.91$ to $-0.95$ in Pearson correlation, and even after removing the trend per run the correlation remains at $-0.60$ to $-0.70$. This allows for a cheap online Edge-of-Stability estimate of the slow sharpness component. The employed probing mechanism searches along Adam's first-step update direction, at initialisation and nine times over the course of the first 50 optimiser steps. The learning-rate cap is set as twice the smallest observed step size, and in the studied learning-rate ranges ($10^{-3}$ to $3.0$) and GPT-2 pretraining experiments all capped runs avoid divergence; in the general architecture analysis, one MLP architecture is still sensitive to the initial batch order. This probing protocol incurs an approximately one percent overhead, and using a non-binding cap means that the optimiser's state and first update are bit-identical. There is no fine-tuning of any of the protocol parameters to any specific architecture; this is the sense in which this is a calibration-free safeguard. It is meant as a way of avoiding divergence, not achieving accuracy. At GPT-2 scale, multiple measurements also illustrate why an initialisation-only cap is insufficient: directional curvature rises substantially in the first five optimiser steps, which motivates the short probationary window.

title: LSD-SMOTE: Latent Semantics Disentangle SMOTE for Imbalanced Data Over-sampling
abstract: Class imbalance is a pervasive and challenging issue in machine learning and data mining, where standard classifiers lean heavily toward the majority class. Although the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) is widely used to mitigate this problem, generating synthetic samples directly in the original high-dimensional feature space often introduces noise, cross-class blending, and unrealistic combinations due to the intricate coupling and non-linear correlations of raw features. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling framework named Latent Semantics Disentangle SMOTE (LSD-SMOTE). The proposed method leverages a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) integrated with a beta-disentanglement penalty to map high-dimensional minority samples into a lower-dimensional latent space, forcing the latent variables to decouple into mutually independent semantic factors. By performing linear interpolation within this decoupled latent space, SMOTE can smoothly manipulate individual semantic axes without causing structural distortion. Finally, a trained decoder reconstructs these newly synthesized latent vectors back into high-quality, diverse minority samples within the original feature space. By decoupling the underlying semantics before generation, LSD-SMOTE effectively prevents the generation of ambiguous boundary samples and enhances the classification performance on imbalanced datasets.

title: Assertion-Contingent Topology Displacement in Multimodal LLM Tutoring: A Controlled Study
abstract: This project reports a controlled study of "assertion-contingent topology displacement" in multimodal LLM tutoring: a failure mode in which a vision-capable model correctly reads a circuit diagram, but a short, confidently wrong user assertion about the circuit's topology displaces that correct reading — producing a fluent, internally consistent derivation of the wrong answer. Across 945 controlled trials, the effect is channel-specific: displacement occurs in 42.7% of visual-diagram trials versus 0% of matched text-based trials describing the identical circuit (Fisher's exact p ≈ 5×10⁻¹⁹). The effect is directional (assert-wrong > neutral doubt > assert-right) and scales with diagram ambiguity, distinguishing it from generic sycophancy or hallucination. We term this "false coherence" — a locally valid derivation built on a displaced premise — and discuss implications for AI-assisted tutoring and human-AI interaction safety.

title: Posterior uncertainty for kernel density estimates
abstract: Recent work in predictive Bayesian inference has enabled novel Bayesian interpretations of many well-known stochastic one-step-ahead predictive algorithms. In this paper, we study classic kernel density estimation in the predictive Bayesian framework. We prove that their predictive measures converge weakly almost surely $\unicode{x2013}$ meaning that their associated predictive resampling sequences are almost surely asymptotically exchangeable $\unicode{x2013}$ and we provide estimators for moments of the limiting random probability measure. We also show that the resampling sequences do not satisfy standard assumptions like being conditionally identically distributed (c.i.d.) or almost c.i.d. (a.c.i.d.), thus providing a non-trivial example of a predictive sequence which is not a.c.i.d. but nevertheless converges weakly almost surely. For Gaussian kernels, we show that the limiting directing measure is almost surely absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, meaning it emits a probability density. This enables us to derive credibility intervals for kernel density estimates, which we illustrate on two real datasets.

title: Label-guided data augmentation for cross-domain aspect-based sentiment analysis via enhanced affinity fusion
abstract: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) aims to identify opinion targets and determine the sentiment polarity expressed toward each aspect, which requires fine-grained modeling of aspect–opinion relations. Despite recent advances, cross-domain ABSA remains challenging due to structural mismatches across domains and the scarcity of high-quality labeled data in target domains. Existing methods often struggle to jointly address relational modeling errors and data sparsity, particularly under low-resource and cross-domain settings. To tackle these challenges, we propose a structure- and data-co-enhanced framework for cross-domain ABSA. At the model level, we introduce an Enhanced Affinity Fusion (EAF) module that explicitly strengthens aspect–opinion relational modeling by selectively integrating complementary attention mechanisms. Specifically, EAF combines biaffine attention to capture second-order interactions with syntax-aware attention to inject structural inductive bias, enabling robust modeling of long-distance dependencies without introducing excessive architectural complexity. At the data level, we propose Label-Guided Data Amplification (LGDA), which enhances supervision diversity and domain robustness through label-driven text expansion, hard sample mining, and domain-adaptive sampling. By jointly enhancing structural representation learning and training data supervision, the proposed framework effectively alleviates both aspect–opinion mismatches and cross-domain data sparsity. Extensive experiments on benchmark ABSA datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain scenarios. Ablation studies further validate the complementary contributions of EAF and LGDA.

title: Setting the Privacy Budget in Differential Privacy by Bounding Adversaries' Odds of Learning Sensitive Information
abstract: Differential privacy is a mathematical definition of what it means to protect data subjects' privacy in data releases. Differential privacy depends on a parameter $ε$ known as the privacy budget. The value of $\varepsilon$ determines the nature of the privacy guarantee, with smaller values generally offering more privacy. However, reducing $\varepsilon$ also tends to decrease the accuracy of results protected with differentially private algorithms. Setting a value for $\varepsilon$ that satisfactorily balances this risk/accuracy trade off is complicated in practice, and there is not a standard approach to doing so. In part this is because practitioners may struggle to understand the privacy guarantee afforded by $\varepsilon$. We present an approach to interpreting and setting $\varepsilon$ in which (i) the practitioner establishes bounds on the posterior odds that adversaries can learn sensitive information, and (ii) the practitioner converts these bounds to values of $\varepsilon$. We illustrate the approach using data from a case control study.

title: MedPlain: Local, Bilingual Plain-Language Simplification of Clinical Text with a Faithfulness Check
abstract: MedPlain is an open-source, locally-run tool that simplifies clinical text into plain language at a chosen reading level, in English and Arabic, and applies a two-layer faithfulness check to surface changed, added, or missing facts for human review. It runs entirely on-device via a local language model (Ollama), reads printed prescriptions from PDF or image, and refuses to simplify low-confidence OCR to guard against hallucination. Evaluation across five clinical specialties shows sharp readability improvement (reading grade ~21 to ~7) and ~95% preservation of numeric facts, while documenting an important limitation: the semantic checker misses most subtle meaning-level distortions, so human review remains necessary. On handwritten documents, OCR failure can combine with model hallucination to produce fluent but fabricated output, which MedPlain mitigates with a confidence gate. MedPlain is a research and educational prototype, not a medical device. It does not provide medical advice, diagnosis, or interpretation.

abstract: Class imbalance is a fundamental bottleneck that severely restricts the generalization performance of classification models in machine learning and data mining. Conventional minority over-sampling techniques, such as standard SMOTE and its variations, synthesize new instances by merely focusing on local neighborhood linear relationships. Consequently, they inevitably overlook the intrinsic "data signature structure" embedded in high-dimensional spaces or non-linear manifolds, which reflects the underlying physical mechanisms or generative dynamics of the minority class. Such destruction of the global topology or essential feature structures often leads to model overfitting, blurred decision boundaries, and the introduction of distribution noise. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling methodology for ultra-imbalanced datasets, termed Signature-preserving SMOTE (SPS-MOTE). The proposed method first extracts the characteristic signature matrix of the minority class by calculating global path integrals, high-order moments, or algebraic invariants of the manifold. During the sample synthesis phase, a collaborative projection mechanism based on conditional matrix decomposition is introduced. This constraint ensures that the newly synthesized samples not only maintain local randomness within their neighborhoods but also strictly adhere to the global signature constraints of the original minority distribution. Extensive classification experiments conducted on various benchmark datasets and domain-specific datasets with strong physical backgrounds demonstrate that SPS-MOTE significantly outperforms classic SMOTE, ADASYN, and Borderline-SMOTE across multiple evaluation metrics, including F1-score, G-mean, and AUC. The theoretical and empirical results indicate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates overfitting, expands minority class representation without generating distribution distortion, and opens up a new paradigm for topology- and geometry-preserving imbalanced data mining.

title: KIR-SMOTE: Knowledge Inconsistency Repair SMOTE for Imbalanced Data Classification
abstract: Class imbalance is a pervasive challenge in machine learning, where standard classifiers often exhibit a strong bias toward the majority class. Although the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) is widely used to address this issue by interpolating new minority samples, it heavily relies on spatial geometry and ignores underlying domain knowledge or logical rules. Consequently, traditional SMOTE frequently synthesizes invalid samples that contain logical contradictions or exacerbate class overlap. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling algorithm termed Knowledge Inconsistency Repair SMOTE (KIR-SMOTE). Instead of strictly avoiding imperfect samples during generation, the core strategy of KIR-SMOTE is to initially allow the creation of "slightly inconsistent samples" to preserve data diversity at the decision boundaries. We establish a formal rule-based knowledge base and define a comprehensive violation index to measure the logical consistency of synthetic samples. Samples exceeding a specific inconsistency threshold are discarded as noise, while those with minor violations are retained and funneled into a dynamic consistency repair mechanism. This mechanism formulates a constrained optimization problem to fine-tune non-core features, minimizing feature perturbation while successfully restoring compliance with domain rules. Synthetic results demonstrate that KIR-SMOTE effectively eliminates semantic contradictions and pseudo-features without sacrificing sample diversity. This approach bridges the gap between geometric interpolation and semantic validity, offering enhanced generalization performance and robust compliance for imbalanced data classification in knowledge-intensive domains such as medical diagnosis and financial fraud detection.

title: Development of A BB84-Based Quantum Security System
abstract: The rapid advancement of quantum computing poses a serious threat to traditional cryptographic systems such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), which rely on computational difficulty for security. Quantum algorithms like Shor’s and Grover’s have the potential to break or weaken these methods, putting modern communication systems at risk. To address this challenge, this work presents a quantum-safe com-munication framework that combines the BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol with Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) techniques, aiming to ensure secure data exchange in the presence of quantum-capable adversaries. In this system, the BB84 protocol is simulated to enable secure key exchange between two parties over a virtual quantum channel. The generated key is refined through processes such as basis matching, error correction, and privacy amplification using SHA-256 to ensure reliability and secrecy. For secur-ing communication, One-Time Pad (OTP) encryption is used alongside HMAC-SHA3-256 to provide both confidentiality and message integrity. Additionally, file encryption is handled using the XChaCha20-Poly1305 algorithm, selected for its efficiency and strong protection against potential vulnerabilities like nonce reuse. To further enhance security, the framework integrates a hybrid key management approach using the Kyber-512 Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) combined with a Key Deriva-tion Function (KDF), merging classical and quantum-resistant techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the system, achieving a Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) of 2.5% and successful performance in both message and file en-cryption. Overall, this work contributes toward the development of practical and resilient communication systems designed for the emerging quantum era.

title: Penerapan Algoritma Finite State Machine (FSM) dan A* pada Game Horror “Oblation”
abstract: In the horror game genre, tension is built not only through visuals and audio, but also through enemy behavior that responds consistently to player actions. This study aims to implement the Finite State Machine (FSM) algorithm to control enemy behavior and the A* algorithm for pathfinding in the first- person horror game "Oblation". Enemy behavior is modeled into five states, namely Patrol, Chase, Attack, LostTarget, and Jumpscare, while A* determines the enemy's movement path toward the player using a hybrid strategy that prioritizes Line of Sight (LOS) checking. FSM testing was conducted using the black-box method on ten transition scenarios, while A* testing was performed through runtime log analysis. The results show that all FSM transitions produced the expected states with a 100% success rate. In the A* testing, 73.19% of 1,160 calls were resolved directly through LOS, with an average computation time of 0.0743 milliseconds per search, so it did not affect frame rate stability. The combination of FSM and A* proved capable of producing enemy AI that is consistent, realistic, and computationally lightweight, thereby supporting increased tension in survival horror gameplay.

title: Applied Information Space Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents an applied architectural framework bridging the theoretical mechanics of Information Space Dynamics (ISD) with LLM-free semantic graph preprocessing methodologies. While the behavioral state of a Large Language Model (LLM) can be rigorously modeled as motion through a high-dimensional information space—measured via kinematic observables such as velocity, curvature, and torsional resistance—instrumenting these diagnostics in real-time presents a severe computational bottleneck. Relying on standard cloud-based generative models for continuous evaluation incurs massive token costs and network latency. To resolve this constraint, this architecture implements the principles of the LiteSemRAG methodology as a foundational ingestion layer. By delegating structural understanding to local, lightweight embedding models, the pipeline circumvents the need for massive generative models during graph construction. The system dynamically resolves polysemy through spatial clustering and utilizes Markov random walks for context compression, isolating the precise semantic nodes needed to calculate trajectory shifts. This decoupling of structural analysis from the generative phase allows diagnostic instruments to continuously monitor the unified system state vector, structural separation ($\alpha$), and discrete geodesic turning curvature ($\kappa$). Ultimately, this framework provides the operational engine necessary to achieve real-time, deterministic telemetry of LLM cognition and attractor state stability at scale, with zero external token expenditure.

title: FCS-SMOTE: An Enhanced Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique Based on Feature Checksum Constraints
abstract: Class imbalance is a pervasive and challenging issue in machine learning and data mining. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) has been widely adopted to alleviate this problem by performing linear interpolation between minority class samples, thereby mitigating the model bias caused by data imbalance. However, traditional SMOTE and its variants focus exclusively on the geometric proximity within the feature space, completely neglecting the underlying algebraic constraints, conservation laws, or specific feature checksum relationships commonly found in real-world applications. Consequently, the synthesized virtual samples frequently violate intrinsic business logic and become "physically impossible" noise, which ultimately degrades the generalization performance of classifiers. To address this critical limitation, this paper proposes an enhanced SMOTE algorithm based on feature checksum constraints, termed Feature Checksum SMOTE (FCS-SMOTE). The core idea of the proposed algorithm is to integrate an explicit feature checksum validation mechanism into the synthetic sampling process through feature space decoupling. The algorithm segregates the original feature space into an independent feature subspace and a dependent checksum subspace. During over-sampling, linear interpolation is restricted solely within the independent subspace to guarantee safety. Subsequently, the values of the dependent checksum features for the new virtual samples are precisely reconstructed via predefined algebraic constraint equations rather than interpolation. This mechanism inherently guarantees that every generated sample strictly adheres to the established business rules and mathematical laws. This paper elaborates on the mathematical formulation, algorithmic framework, and optimization strategies of FCS-SMOTE. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the algorithm can eliminate 100% of invalid synthetic samples while effectively preserving the statistical distribution of the minority class. FCS-SMOTE not only extends the theoretical boundaries of traditional synthetic sampling methodologies but also provides a robust, compliant, and practical data augmentation solution for industries with stringent data compliance requirements, such as financial fraud detection, industrial equipment fault diagnosis, and clinical medical decision-making.

title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.

title: Official Symbolic Identity of the Cesar Sosa Cognitive Framework Series (CS-CFS): Official Symbolic System, Graphic Work, and Epistemological Architecture
abstract: This report documents the Official Symbolic Identity of the Cesar Sosa Cognitive Framework Series (CS-CFS), establishing the official conceptual interpretation of its visual identity. Beyond documenting the original graphic work, this publication formally defines the symbolic architecture associated with the CS-CFS, describing the epistemological meaning of each visual component and its role within the framework's theoretical structure. The document serves as the canonical reference for the official symbolic system of the CS-CFS and its institutional visual identity. The symbolic identity integrates principles of cognition, compatible cognitive communication, Human–Artificial Intelligence cognitive ecologies, knowledge construction, and epistemological architecture. This publication is intended for scientific documentation, institutional use, academic citation, and long-term preservation. The official symbolic interpretation of the CS-CFS visual identity is documented in the Zenodo report "Official Symbolic Identity of the Cesar Sosa Cognitive Framework Series (CS-CFS): Official Symbolic System, Graphic Work, and Epistemological Architecture" (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21199667).

title: Selective Quantum Zeno Protection in Fock Space via Geometric Tensor \Xi
abstract: We demonstrate the emergent suppression of decoherence in a dispersive qubit-cavity system by introducing a geometric dissipative channel derived from the \Xi tensor. Numerical integration of the Lindblad master equation within an extended Fock space (N=40) reveals a 40% reduction in the effective dephasing rate, corresponding to a 1.6x extension of T_2. This phenomenon stems from the selective damping of high photon-number components, inducing a cavity-state-dependent Quantum Zeno effect that freezes the qubit's phase diffusion without requiring external active control.

title: Information-loss Controlled SMOTE for Imbalanced Data Learning
abstract: Data imbalance is a prevalent and challenging problem in machine learning, where classifiers often perform poorly due to the significant underrepresentation of minority class samples. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) alleviates this issue by generating synthetic samples through linear interpolation. However, the blind interpolation mechanism of traditional SMOTE frequently leads to geometric topology distortion, blurred decision boundaries, and noise generation. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an improved over-sampling algorithm termed Information-Loss Controlled SMOTE (ILC-SMOTE). The proposed method formulates the synthetic sample generation as an external perturbation to the original feature space and establishes a dual-constrained information loss measurement framework. On the local scale, a geometric structure loss metric based on locally linear embedding is introduced to preserve the underlying manifold structure. On the global scale, a probability distribution distortion metric utilizing kernel density estimation and Kullback-Leibler divergence is integrated to maintain statistical consistency. An adaptive admission control mechanism is then implemented to filter out candidate samples that introduce unacceptable information loss. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that ILC-SMOTE effectively prevents the generation of cross-boundary noise, preserves the original geometric skeleton, and ensures asymptotic distribution convergence, thereby significantly enhancing classification performance in complex, non-linear spaces.

title: An Equivalence-Class Based Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (EC-SMOTE) for Sample Redistribution in Imbalanced Data Classification
abstract: In machine learning and data mining, class imbalance presents a significant challenge to traditional classification algorithms, which often bias towards the majority class and suffer from low recognition rates on the minority class. Although the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) is widely applied to mitigate this issue, its reliance on blind local linear interpolation often amplifies noise, introduces the "bridge" phenomenon across distinct clusters, and blurs decision boundaries. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling algorithm named Equivalence-Class Based SMOTE (EC-SMOTE). By incorporating the concept of equivalence classes from algebraic topology and rough set theory, the proposed algorithm partitions the minority feature space into mutually exclusive equivalence-class structures based on an adaptive neighborhood relationship and its transitive closure. Three core attributes—Size Metric (SM), Boundary Danger Metric (BDM), and Spatial Scattering Metric (SSM)—are formulated to quantitatively evaluate each equivalence class. This mathematical framework filters out isolated noise and dynamically redistributes synthetic sample quotas to reinforce boundaries and fill inner gaps seamlessly. Furthermore, a topology-preserving synthesis strategy is introduced, which constrains interpolation within the same equivalence class and applies a centripetal force toward the cluster center. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that EC-SMOTE effectively prevents over-fitting and maintains the intrinsic geometric structure of the minority manifold, thereby establishing robust and distinct decision boundaries for improved classification performance.

title: High-Fidelity One-Step Generative Visuomotor Policy via Recursive Correction, Frequency Consistency, and Contrastive Flow Matching
abstract: Generative models such as diffusion and flow matching have advanced robotic visuomotor policies by modeling multimodal action distributions, but their multi-step sampling or ODE solving introduces inference latency. Existing one-step acceleration methods often compress the whole generation process into a single large update, leading to spatial deviation, frequency distortion, and mode averaging. This paper proposes a high-fidelity one-step generative visuomotor policy framework that addresses these issues with three complementary mechanisms. Recursive Consistent Action Flow (RCAF) uses recursive correction to compensate for spatial truncation errors and align one-step predictions with refined flow trajectories. Dual-Timestep Frequency Consistency (DTFC) preserves high-frequency manipulation details through adaptive spectral consistency across flow timesteps. Contrastive Flow Matching (CFM) separates entangled action flows with a margin-based repulsive objective, reducing ambiguous actions in multimodal manipulation. Experiments on RoboTwin, RoboTwin 2.0, Adroit, DexArt, and real-world robot platforms show that the proposed method achieves competitive or superior performance compared with strong 10-step generative policy baselines while requiring only one forward pass (1 NFE), enabling low-latency visuomotor control.

Recursive Consistent Action Flow (RCAF) uses recursive correction to compensate for spatial truncation errors and align one-step predictions with refined flow trajectories. Dual-Timestep Frequency Consistency (DTFC) preserves high-frequency manipulation details through adaptive spectral consistency across flow timesteps. Contrastive Flow Matching (CFM) separates entangled action flows with a margin-based repulsive objective, reducing ambiguous actions in multimodal manipulation. Experiments on RoboTwin, RoboTwin 2.0, Adroit, DexArt, and real-world robot platforms show that the proposed method achieves competitive or superior performance compared with strong 10-step generative policy baselines while requiring only one forward pass (1 NFE), enabling low-latency visuomotor control.

title: ПОРІВНЯЛЬНИЙ АНАЛІЗ АЛГОРИТМІВ ОПТИМІЗАЦІЇ ТА НАВЧАННЯ ЗІ ЗМІШАНОЮ ТОЧНІСТЮ ДЛЯ МІНІМІЗАЦІЇ ЧАСУ НАВЧАННЯ НЕЙРОННИХ МЕРЕЖ
abstract: Topicality. The rapid growth of deep learning applications has placed training time among the most critical engineering constraints in neural network development. Modern architectures such as ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2 require substantial computational resources even for compact benchmarks, making training efficiency a pressing problem for researchers with limited hardware budgets. The subject of study is the combined effect of three first-order optimization algorithms — SGD with momentum, Adam, and AdamW – together with automatic mixed-precision (FP16/FP32) arithmetic on per-epoch training time, GPU memory consumption, and classification accuracy. The purpose of the article is to quantify and compare six optimizers × precision configurations on a consumer-grade GPU to identify the combination that minimizes training time subject to a 1 % accuracy tolerance. The following results were obtained. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX 3060 Ti with ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2 trained on CIFAR-10 for 100 epochs showed that AdamW with PyTorch AMP reduced per-epoch training time by 29–31 % relative to SGD FP32 while improving validation accuracy by 1.5–2.5 percentage points. Peak GPU memory decreased by approximately 30 % under AMP. Conclusion. Decoupled weight decay combined with half-precision tensor arithmetic is an effective strategy for minimizing neural network training time on modern consumer GPUs. The results provide a reproducible benchmark and motivate further research into adaptive optimizer switching and cross-platform energy-efficiency metrics.

title: Discrete-State Transition SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique Based on State Machine and Trajectory Evolution for Imbalanced Discrete Data
abstract: Class imbalance is a pervasive and challenging issue in machine learning and data mining, often leading conventional classifiers to favor the majority class and fail to recognize minority patterns. While the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) has achieved remarkable success in continuous numeric spaces, it exhibits inherent limitations when dealing with discrete features, categorical states, or sequential data governed by underlying transition logics. Traditional linear interpolation in Euclidean space frequently yields synthesized values devoid of physical meaning and disrupts the chronological or causal dependencies between features. To overcome these deficiencies, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling paradigm named Discrete-state transition SMOTE (DST-SMOTE). The proposed algorithm conceptualizes high-dimensional discrete samples as temporal or causal trajectory paths within a finite state machine framework. By aggregating transition frequencies across the minority class, we construct a global state transition probability matrix that mathematically formalizes the underlying dynamics of the minority data distribution. Furthermore, a novel State Transition Divergence Distance (STDD) is developed to measure topological similarities between discrete state sequences without relying on Euclidean metrics. Virtual samples are then generated via a strategic mechanism combining probabilistic random walks and cross-recombination under structural compatibility constraints. A comprehensive mathematical framework is established to evaluate the theoretical validity of DST-SMOTE. We rigorously prove the consistency of the stationary distribution between the synthesized and original minority samples using Markov chain convergence theorems. We further demonstrate the topological safety boundary of the synthesized sequences within directed state graphs and derive the generalization error bound based on statistical learning theory, confirming that the algorithm effectively tightens the generalization upper bound of downstream classifiers. Analytical discussions also reveal that the algorithm maintains a low time and space complexity while inherently exhibiting strong robust immunity against localized label noise and outliers. DST-SMOTE offers a theoretically sound and industrially viable solution for class imbalance in state-driven domains such as financial fraud detection, network intrusion prevention, and clinical pathway modeling.

title: An Over-Sampling Algorithm Based on Jumping Between Different Abstraction Levels (Abstraction-level SMOTE)
abstract: In the field of machine learning and data mining, class imbalance is a widespread challenge that severely compromises the classification performance of minority samples. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and its variants address this by performing linear interpolation within the original feature space. However, when dealing with complex, high-dimensional, and non-linear manifold distributions, these methods are prone to "blind interpolation," which generates synthesized samples that overlap with the majority class or destroy the inherent boundary structures. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel over-sampling paradigm named Abstraction-level SMOTE. Instead of operating within a single static feature space, the proposed framework establishes a cross-level jumping mechanism formalized as "Low-level Space -> High-level Space -> Interpolation -> Low-level Space". The algorithm first maps the low-level original minority samples into a high-level abstract semantic space through a non-linear encoder function z_i = E(x_i). Due to the manifold-flattening effect of deep representations, the complex data distribution becomes smoother and more linearly separable in the high-level space. Synthetic abstract representations are then generated by performing linear interpolation between an abstract sample and its nearest neighbors: z_new = z_i + alpha * (z_zi - z_i). Finally, a backward reconstruction decoder function x_new = D(z_new) is utilized to project the synthesized hidden variables back to the low-level physical feature space, producing realistic virtual minority samples that conform to the original data manifold. Theoretical analysis indicates that Abstraction-level SMOTE effectively breaks the non-linear barriers of traditional methods, mitigates the interference of low-level noise, and preserves both macroscopic semantic trends and microscopic feature details. This method offers a robust solution for learning from imbalanced data with intricate underlying manifold structures.

title: FedACT: Federated Adaptive Coordinate Trust Modulation for Robust Transformer Training under Data Heterogeneity
abstract: Federated Transformer training increasingly relies on local AdamW, whose adaptive updates can provide much stronger local progress than SGD-based training. However, under heterogeneous client data, even globally corrected AdamW updates may remain highly uneven in coordinate-wise reliability. We refer to this phenomenon as coordinate trust mismatch. Existing federated adaptive optimizers mainly address mismatch at the client-update or communication-round level, but still apply the corrected adaptive direction densely and uniformly across coordinates. In this paper, we propose FedACT, a global-aware coordinate trust modulation method for federated AdamW training. FedACT first forms a globally corrected adaptive direction and then reallocates update magnitudes according to a coordinate-wise trust score, assigning larger steps to coordinates jointly supported by local gradients and global correction, while preserving smaller non-zero updates on the remaining coordinates. Extensive experiments on federated vision Transformers, CNNs, LLM pre-training, and LLM fine-tuning show that FedACT consistently improves over strong federated adaptive baselines, with the largest gains on Transformer models under stronger data heterogeneity. Mechanism analyses further show that FedACT improves cross-client direction consistency, suggesting that coordinate-level trust allocation effectively complements round-level global-local correction. Code will be released.

title: Domain Adaptation in Low-Resource Perso-Arabic ASR with XLSR-53 Pre-Training
abstract: Self-supervised pre-training could effectively improve the performance of low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR). title: LLM Evaluation Toolkit: Reliability, Adversarial Testing, and Judge Calibration for LLM Systems
abstract: LLM Evaluation Toolkit is an open-source research toolkit for building more reliable evaluation pipelines for large language model (LLM) systems. The toolkit approaches LLM evaluation as a measurement problem rather than a purely benchmarking problem. It provides tools and experimental components for studying evaluation reliability, adversarial behavior during evaluation, and calibration of LLM-based judges. Main components include: • Reliability analysis for measuring evaluation stability and score variance • Adversarial evaluation experiments for detecting evaluation awareness and metric gaming • Judge calibration tools, including inter-rater agreement, Cohen's kappa, and judge drift analysis The project is intended for researchers, ML engineers, and AI practitioners interested in trustworthy AI, evaluation validity, and reliable LLM systems. Developed within the LLM Measurement Lab initiative.

title: Preregistered Amplitude-Scaling and Multi-Vector Adjudication of a QRT-Consistent Coherence Result on Superconducting Hardware (v4.2)
abstract: A preregistered Ramsey test (v4.1, job d94hi4lgc6cc73ff4cc0, ibm_fez, July 2026) of Quantum Resonance Theory's coherence-enhancement prediction (Anson 2024, DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263717) returned a QRT-consistent result: G_A = +2.87%, 95% CI [+2.35%, +3.46%], at the theory-designated ωr = 10 MHz with R0 = 10⁻³ rad. Per that registration's own terms, the result is treated as an artifact until it survives escalation. This study executes the highest-information single-session adjudication available within remaining hardware quota, exploiting two facts: (1) a genuine drive-coupled effect must scale with drive amplitude, while calibration-floor and noise-spectrum artifacts at milliradian angles do not — so a 10× amplitude arm converts a marginal effect into a decisively resolvable one; (2) the packed six-qubit layout carries six conditions per circuit, so amplitude scaling, second-device replication at original amplitude, neighbor peak structure, drive-phase randomization, and an undriven reference all execute in the same 24 circuits. The primary decision rests on the amplitude arm alone; all other vectors are declared secondary and descriptive. The backend is required in code to differ from ibm_fez (the v4.1 device). The result will be published regardless of outcome.

title: РЕАЛІЗАЦІЯ ТА ОЦІНЮВАННЯ КВАНТОВОГО ГЕНЕРАТОРА ВИПАДКОВИХ ЧИСЕЛ НА ОСНОВІ ANU QRNG ДЛЯ КРИПТОГРАФІЧНИХ ЗАСТОСУВАНЬ
abstract: Topicality. Reliable random number generation is one of the key requirements for modern cryptographic systems and cybersecurity applications. Traditional pseudo-random number generators are based on deterministic algorithms and may exhibit limited entropy and predictability, which can negatively affect information security. The subject of study in the article is methods of quantum random number generation and approaches to evaluating the quality of generated random sequences. The purpose of the article is to analyze modern methods of quantum random number generation, develop a software tool for obtaining quantum random numbers based on the ANU Quantum Random Number Generator service, perform statistical testing of the generated sequences, and analyze the obtained results. The following results were obtained. Modern quantum random number generation systems were analyzed and compared. A software tool was implemented in Python for automatic retrieval of quantum random numbers through the ANU QRNG API. The generated binary sequences were evaluated using Frequency Test and Block Frequency Test from the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite. The obtained p-values were 0.977181 and 0.200659 respectively, confirming successful completion of both tests. Additionally, visual analysis of the generated sequences revealed no noticeable patterns or repetitive structures. Conclusion. The obtained results confirm the high quality of quantum random sequences generated using ANU QRNG and demonstrate the applicability of the developed software tool for cryptographic and cybersecurity applications requiring high-quality randomness.
